drafts.raw_submission: We the people demand end to end transparency for all govt. funded contracts... we need the private organizations finances as related to the government contracts... that's the end game for the only true transparency of knowing where every dollar lands.
drafts.neutral_framing: Should Clark County require end-to-end public reporting — who received the money, what it bought, and what it achieved — as a written condition of every contract, grant, and incentive the county funds?
drafts.final_wording: Should every dollar of Clark County government money — spent directly or passed through to any organization — be publicly traceable down to the receipt: who was paid, how much, and for what?
drafts.final_wording_note: Final wording chosen by the submitter on 2026-07-18, per the ownership rule. The neutral framing above was offered; the submitter chose the receipt-level version.
shaping_notes: The neutral framing converts a demand into a yes/no question an official body could actually act on, per the charter. The submitter chooses the final wording; both versions are logged per the Idea Shaper ownership rules.

Mechanism honesty: a county cannot open a private company's books. It CAN condition its own money — disclosure clauses in contracts and incentive agreements, and Arkansas courts have applied the FOIA to private entities substantially supported by public funds. The question is framed around what the county can lawfully require.

The evidence base is this corpus: $1.84M/year in EDCCC incentives with no public recipient list, commodity vendors absent from any posted record, an ambulance contract whose terms never appeared in public, and a state rebate mechanism that hides claimants. All documented, none illegal — the question is whether residents want the county to require more than the law's minimum.

Pre-vote checklist per the charter: neutrality review, human review against bright lines (no named-individual conduct — this is a policy question, clears), official partner conversation (county judge / quorum court are the actors), and conflict-of-interest disclosure: the platform's sponsor and founder is a county business owner; that relationship is disclosed on the issue page.
drafts.tier_note: Open as a Tier 0 sentiment poll during the site's quiet launch: no account, one voice per browser, changeable until close. Per the charter, Tier 0 is displayed but never cited as verified resident opinion — verification tiers arrive with the full voting layer.

requested_documents.title: The EDCCC incentive recipients and their performance terms
requested_documents.why: $1,844,538 a year in economic-development incentives, with no public list of who got it or what they promised. It sits on the money trail as a dead end.

requested_documents.title: How fire protection is funded, and the coverage map
requested_documents.why: How fire is paid for and which areas it covers — the honest basis for any fire-funding question.

requested_documents.title: The roughly $1.3 million state sales-tax rebate repayment
requested_documents.why: Local reporting says the county owes the state about $1.3M in rebate repayments — a news lead the county’s own records would confirm or correct.

requested_documents.title: The county ambulance / EMS service agreement
requested_documents.why: The terms of the county’s emergency-medical-service contract never appeared in a public document.

drafts.background: This platform traced every public dollar it could. Most of the trail is documented: the money trail cross-foots to the dollar, and what the auditors reported is quoted in full. But parts of the trail stop short of a receipt: $1.84M/year in economic development incentives with no public recipient list, commodity purchases no posted document names, and about $4M a year that moves without public detail. This question asks whether that should change — not whether anyone did anything wrong.
drafts.disclosure: This question was submitted by the platform’s founder, who owns Ozark Cleaners — the platform’s sponsor. That double relationship is disclosed here on purpose.

founding_solutions.title: Pay procurement from line-attributed accounts, so the check register publishes itself
founding_solutions.summary: Move the county’s discretionary/procurement spending onto authorized accounts tied to each budget line — virtual cards or ring-fenced accounts — whose transaction feed publishes by default. The receipt is then generated by the payment itself, not reconstructed later from records requests. This is proven infrastructure: a federal card rail (GSA SmartPay) already captures line-item transaction data at $39B+/year, one state (Oklahoma) already publishes item-level card transactions, and governments already ring-fence each line in the ledger (encumbrance accounting). Honest limit: it reaches only the ~15–30% of a budget that is operating procurement — not payroll, debt, or transfers — which is exactly where the county’s dead ends are today (the $1.84M “INCENTIVES” line). Framed as audit-and-anti-diversion, not programmable control.

citations.label: GSA SmartPay FY2025 statistics ($39.4B, ~82M transactions, Level 3 line-item data)
Oklahoma — item-level purchase-card transactions published by default
Encumbrance accounting — how governments already ring-fence each appropriation line
GAO-08-333 — the honest downside: 41–48% of purchase-card transactions failed basic controls

founding_solutions.title: Publish the county check register — downloadable and searchable, the way Tarrant County does
founding_solutions.summary: Right now Clark County publishes no public check register at all (Docket #10) — “who got paid” is a dead end on the money trail. The immediately-doable fix, needing no new payment rails: post every check the county writes — payee, amount, date, and purpose — as downloadable data with a vendor lookup, not a PDF. There is a clear peer model to copy: Tarrant County, Texas — the only county in its state to earn all six of the state’s transparency stars — publishes a downloadable check register (down to an item-description field) plus a live vendor-payment lookup anyone can search. Oklahoma goes a step further and publishes purchase-card spending at the item level; Ohio put 112 million transactions online and went from 46th to 1st in national transparency. Clark can copy the floor — a downloadable, searchable register — this year, from the accounting system it already runs, and this platform can ingest the feed directly instead of chasing records.

citations.label: Tarrant County, TX — downloadable check register (with item-description field) + live vendor-payment lookup
Tarrant County — live vendor payment lookup
Oklahoma — item-level purchase-card transactions published by default (the stretch goal)
OhioCheckbook — 112M transactions online; Ohio went from 46th to 1st in transparency

drafts.neutral_framing: Should Clark County treat access to food as shared public infrastructure — supporting community food-growing (gardens on public land, a gleaning and produce-sharing network, and school and campus gardens) the way it supports parks, the library, and water?
drafts.final_wording: Should Clark County back growing and sharing food together as public infrastructure — gardens on public land, a gleaning and produce-sharing network, and school and campus gardens — the way it backs parks, the library, and water?
drafts.final_wording_note: Opened by the platform’s founder during the site’s quiet launch. A neutral framing and this plain wording are both logged per the Idea Shaper ownership rules; the plain version was chosen.
shaping_notes: This is a policy question a county body could act on — not a named-individual conduct question and not an active ballot measure. It clears the charter’s bright lines.

Mechanism honesty: a county cannot guarantee anyone’s food, and this question does not claim it can. It asks whether the county should back community food-growing as ongoing infrastructure — land, coordination, and grant-seeking — the parts a county actually controls.

The evidence base is cited in full on the /food brief and inside each founding solution, with verification caveats stated in the open (some figures are corroborated secondary sources, and are flagged as such rather than presented as primary).

drafts.background: About one in five people in Clark County are food insecure — a 20% rate in the 2023 Feeding America Map the Meal Gap estimate, above Arkansas’s 19% and the nation’s 14% (source). Most food help is emergency help, and that work is essential — nothing here replaces it. This question asks about a second, cheaper, more durable thing: whether the county should back growing and sharing food together as public infrastructure, using land, know-how, and grant money it largely already has — a Cooperative Extension office in every county, a statewide gleaning network in all 75 counties, and two universities in town. The full research, with precedents and honest limits, is in Food as a utility.
drafts.disclosure: This question was opened by the platform’s founder. Unlike the contract-transparency question, no sponsor relationship is at stake here; it is disclosed only because the platform names who opens every question.

founding_solutions.title: Open unused public land for community gardens — a $1 lease, not a land sale
founding_solutions.summary: Clark County and its cities hold vacant parcels. Offer them for community gardens through a simple, revocable license — the model Newark runs at $1 a year and Baltimore runs for free — so no land is ever sold or given away. This is a proven public service, not an experiment: Seattle has run 91 community gardens through a city department since 1973 (its gardeners donated 40,000 pounds of produce to meal programs in 2023), and Brown County, Wisconsin has run 13 gardens and 386 plots through its Extension office, the county, and the city since 1996. The know-how is already here and free — every Arkansas county has a Cooperative Extension office and the Master Gardener program behind it. Honest limit: land is necessary but not sufficient. Gardens need water, soil, and stewards, and a plot supplements a household’s groceries (a California study estimates about $435 of produce a season), it does not end anyone’s food insecurity.

citations.label: Seattle P-Patch — 91 city-run community gardens since 1973; 40,000 lb donated in 2023
Brown County, WI — county + Extension community gardens (13 gardens, 386 plots) since 1996
Newark Adopt-a-Lot — $1/year lease of city land for gardening
Baltimore Adopt-A-Lot — free, revocable license for community gardens
Arkansas Master Gardener Program — free Extension horticulture support in every county

founding_solutions.title: Plug into the Arkansas Gleaning Project and a produce-sharing network
founding_solutions.summary: Do not build gleaning from scratch — it already runs statewide. The Arkansas Gleaning Project (the Arkansas Hunger Relief Alliance with the Society of St. Andrew) has gleaned more than 12 million pounds of fresh produce and works with 800-plus hunger-relief organizations across all 75 counties. The county’s job is connection: route surplus from gardens, farms, and the farmers market into that network, and set up a community fridge or produce-sharing point for daily give-and-take. Nearly free — the logistics already exist. Honest limit: community fridges are citizen-led mutual aid, not a government program (the national Freedge network counted 150-plus US fridges in 2021). A county can host or tolerate one, but volunteers keep it running, not staff.

citations.label: Arkansas Gleaning Project — 12M+ lb gleaned, 800+ organizations, all 75 counties
Community fridges (Freedge model) — citizen-led mutual aid, 150+ US fridges (2021)

founding_solutions.title: Grow it in the schools and on the two campuses
founding_solutions.summary: Clark County has assets most rural counties do not: a school district and two universities, Henderson State and Ouachita Baptist. School gardens feed cafeterias and teach kids where food comes from — Denver’s Garden to Cafeteria program put more than 5,000 pounds of school-grown produce into salad bars at about 250 schools. This is not untested here: in 2011 USDA’s People’s Garden School Pilot partnered with the University of Arkansas to build school gardens through Cooperative Extension. The evidence is real but honest about itself — the best systematic review links community gardening to higher fruit-and-vegetable intake while stating plainly that the overall evidence quality is low. We keep that caveat attached rather than oversell it.

citations.label: Denver Garden to Cafeteria — 5,000+ lb of school produce into ~250 school salad bars
USDA People’s Garden School Pilot, partnered with the University of Arkansas (2011)
Hume et al. 2022, BMC Public Health — systematic review (higher F&V intake; “evidence quality overall was low”)

founding_solutions.title: Stand up a food policy council — a standing table, not a new bureaucracy
founding_solutions.summary: A food policy council is a lightweight body a local government can create by resolution to coordinate the people already working on food — growers, schools, the food bank, the universities, and the county itself. Johns Hopkins’ Center for a Livable Future documents that these can be housed directly in government, and at least 283 were active across the US as of 2020. It is the cheap, structural piece that keeps gardens, gleaning, and school plots from staying one-off projects. The north star — honestly out of a county’s scale, but showing the direction: Belo Horizonte runs a coordinated food-as-a-right system at about 2% of its city budget, and Rosario turned vacant land into 2,500 tons of food a year (a WRI Prize for Cities winner). Both are the work of a standing municipal food body, not a single grant.

citations.label: Johns Hopkins Center for a Livable Future — how to structure a food policy council (can be housed in government)
CDC — 283 food policy councils active in the US as of 2020
Belo Horizonte — municipal food-as-a-right system at ~2% of city budget
Rosario, Argentina — urban agriculture (2,500 tons/yr; WRI Prize for Cities, 2021)

founding_solutions.title: Fund it with money that already exists, not new county taxes
founding_solutions.summary: This does not have to come out of the general fund. USDA’s Community Food Projects Competitive Grants Program funds exactly this kind of work — up to $400,000, with a 1-to-1 match — and is open to nonprofits and gleaning groups (a local food nonprofit or the food bank applies, since a county government is not directly eligible for the core track). Extension support is already free to every county. Honest limit: these grants are competitive, time-limited, and need a nonprofit applicant and a match — they are seed money to get a program self-sustaining, not a permanent funding line. The point is that the county’s own cost can be land, coordination, and political will, not a new tax.

citations.label: USDA Community Food Projects Competitive Grants — up to $400,000, 1:1 match, nonprofits/gleaners eligible
Arkansas Master Gardener Program — free Extension support in every county
